extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning news/feature reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting on fires, accidents, and related emergencies for newspapers: present the cause, casualties, official responses, investigation status, and human-interest details in a clear chronological narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the cause of the incident (known or suspected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the apparent cause or likely origin of the fire/accident (e.g., “A glowing match...is believed to have started the fire”), and indicate when cause is suspected rather than confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specifics when available (how the match was used, broken bit on a bridle, torn gasoline tank), and label theories as such. Example language from the page: “A glowing match...is believed to have started the fire” and “At first it was thought that the fire was of incendiary origin.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention indirect or contributing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Include indirect causes or conditions that contributed to the event (poor lighting, kerosene lamps, sidewalks, slippery rails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the mechanism linking the condition to the incident (matches struck in dark halls; kerosene lamps going out; poor lighting forced matches). The page notes: “Poor lighting in the hallways may have been an indirect cause...kerosene lamps were used to light the halls.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify property ownership and occupancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Name owners, managers, and describe occupancy (number of families, location, landlord names and addresses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give owner name and address when known and state how the building was occupied (e.g., “The house was occupied by six families, two on each floor. It is owned by John Korno, a banker, of 667 Grand Street”). This situates responsibility and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: List casualties and injured with specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report deaths and injuries with names, relationships, floors or locations, and counts where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide as much identifying detail as possible (family membership, boarders, ages). Example: “All of the victims were suffocated by smoke. Five were members of the family of Michael Blund...”

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the mechanics of the accident or damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the physical elements produced harm (explosion from gasoline tank, car telescoped, streetcar slid into excavation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the sequence and physical interactions (e.g., “Hanley’s machine ploughed into the rear of the Farley car, tearing a hole in the gasoline tank. The lamps ignited the gasoline and an explosion followed”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include official sources and quoted authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite named officials, investigators, commissioners, and include direct quotations when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use officials to support statements about cause, compliance, law, and investigations (e.g., Tenement House Commissioner John J. Murphy; Colonel William Hayward). The page contains direct quotes such as Commissioner Murphy’s explanation about lighting prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document rescue, medical response, and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Report who rescued victims, which hospitals they were taken to, immediate medical condition, surgeons and nurses involved, and prognosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include actions taken at the scene (fire ladders, ambulances), names of hospitals and doctors, and statements about recovery chances. Example: “Ambulances from all parts of the city were called, and soon there was a force of thirty surgeons and as many more nurses at work.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide chronological narrative of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the sequence from discovery to rescue to investigation in time order so the reader understands how events unfolded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with the immediate discovery/alarm and move step-by-step (alarm turned in → arrival of firemen → rescue → investigation). The pieces in the chapter consistently follow this order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report investigative and legal follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Note ongoing investigations, agencies involved, arrests or missing persons, contract/insurance details, and legal liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List agencies conducting inquiries and any relevant contractual or statutory notes (workmen’s compensation, bonds). Example: “seven independent investigations...by District Attorney Perkins, the Fire Department, the Public Service Commission...” and discussion of contractor bonds and liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe building/equipment compliance and safety features
rubrics_metrics.description: State whether fire escapes, lighting, and other safety installations complied with law or regulation and how that affected outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report inspection findings and compliance status (e.g., “Except with regard to lighting...the burned tenement complied with all the provisions of the law. The fire escapes were as prescribed”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give precise time and location details
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide street addresses, cross streets, times of day, and other geographic/time markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include exact addresses and times (e.g., “shortly before 8 o’clock...between Twenty-third and Twenty-fifth Streets”), which anchors the story and aids verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest details and personal background
rubrics_metrics.description: Add small personal facts or biographies that humanize victims and participants (occupations, age, family ties, notable accomplishments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective background material to make readers care and to show consequences (e.g., lengthy description of George C. Hurlbut’s career as librarian; Mr. Trask’s status as a leading financier). Keep such details relevant and concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report eyewitness accounts and crowd/scene behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Use eyewitness description and note how bystanders and crowds affected rescue or scene conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute eyewitness statements and describe crowd effects (e.g., “flames were seen shooting out of the windows by a passerby, who turned in an alarm” and “so excited was the crowd...it was difficult work”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe property damage and material evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail what was physically destroyed or preserved (cars destroyed, bodies lightly scorched, structural collapse, broken mains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey the visual and material facts to illustrate scale and cause (e.g., “All that was left of the car...was the roof and the steel trucks”; “Before the Nahant fire department could reach the scene both automobiles were destroyed”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention service disruptions and remedial actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report interruption to public services (streetcar suspension, broken mains) and steps taken to restore safety and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List measures taken (shutting off gas mains, closing high-pressure mains, restoring wire service) and temporary orders (tenants ordered to quit houses). Example: “The Seventh Avenue car service was suspended south of Thirty-second Street.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Include technical or policy implications where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, report and quote experts who draw broader safety or policy lessons (e.g., wooden vs steel cars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these comments to connect the incident to possible reforms or debates, but clearly attribute them as opinion (Colonel Hayward’s comment on wooden cars: “If that car...had been a steel car I do not believe a person would have been hurt”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unqualified speculation; present theories and uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting causes or motives that are not established, clearly mark them as theories and present any evidence or reasons they are held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualify early suppositions and explain limits of knowledge (e.g., “It was thought...; the officials were hampered in their investigation because most of the tenants were foreigners and could not speak English”).
